section.paragraph: We have spent considerable time learning how to factor polynomials. We will now look at polynomial equations and solve them using factoring, if possible.
A polynomial equation is an equation that contains a polynomial expression. The degree of the polynomial equation is the degree of the polynomial.

note.title: Polynomial Equation
note.paragraph: A polynomial equation is an equation that contains a polynomial expression.
The degree of the polynomial equation is the degree of the polynomial.

section.paragraph: We have already solved polynomial equations of degree one. Polynomial equations of degree one are linear equations are of the form $$ax + b = c.$$
We are now going to solve polynomial equations of degree two. A polynomial equation of degree two is called a quadratic equation. Listed below are some examples of quadratic equations:
The last equation doesn’t appear to have the variable squared, but when we simplify the expression on the left we will get $$n^{2} + n.$$
The general form of a quadratic equation is $$ax^{2} + bx + c = 0,$$ with $$a \neq 0.$$ (If $$a = 0,$$ then $$0 \cdot x^{2} = 0$$ and we are left with no quadratic term.)

note.title: Quadratic Equation
note.paragraph: An equation of the form $$ax^{2} + bx + c = 0$$ is called a quadratic equation.
$$a,b, \text{and} c \text{are real numbers and} a \neq 0$$

section.paragraph: To solve quadratic equations we need methods different from the ones we used in solving linear equations. We will look at one method here and then several others in a later chapter.
section.heading: Use the Zero Product Property
section.paragraph: We will first solve some quadratic equations by using the Zero Product Property. The Zero Product Property says that if the product of two quantities is zero, then at least one of the quantities is zero. The only way to get a product equal to zero is to multiply by zero itself.

note.title: Zero Product Property
note.paragraph: If $$a \cdot b = 0,$$ then either $$a = 0$$ or $$b = 0$$ or both.

section.paragraph: We will now use the Zero Product Property, to solve a quadratic equation.

section.heading: Solve Quadratic Equations by Factoring
section.paragraph: The Zero Product Property works very nicely to solve quadratic equations. The quadratic equation must be factored, with zero isolated on one side. So we must be sure to start with the quadratic equation in standard form, $$ax^{2} + bx + c = 0.$$ Then we must factor the expression on the left.

Step 2. Factor the quadratic expression.
Step 3. Use the Zero Product Property.
Step 4. Solve the linear equations.
Step 5. Check. Substitute each solution separately into the original equation.

section.paragraph: The Zero Product Property also applies to the product of three or more factors. If the product is zero, at least one of the factors must be zero. We can solve some equations of degree greater than two by using the Zero Product Property, just like we solved quadratic equations.

section.heading: Solve Equations with Polynomial Functions
section.paragraph: As our study of polynomial functions continues, it will often be important to know when the function will have a certain value or what points lie on the graph of the function. Our work with the Zero Product Property will be help us find these answers.

problem.paragraph: ⓐ find x when $$f(x) = 6$$ ⓑ find two points that lie on the graph of the function.

row.cell: Put the quadratic in standard form.
Use the zero product property. Solve.

solution.paragraph: ⓑ Since $$f(-4) = 6$$ and $$f(2) = 6,$$ the points $$\left( {-4,6} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,6} \right)$$ lie on the graph of the function.

section.paragraph: The Zero Product Property also helps us determine where the function is zero. A value of x where the function is 0, is called a zero of the function.

note.title: Zero of a Function
note.paragraph: For any function f, if $$f(x) = 0,$$ then x is a zero of the function.

section.paragraph: When $$f(x) = 0,$$ the point $$\left( {x,0} \right)$$ is a point on the graph. This point is an x-intercept of the graph. It is often important to know where the graph of a function crosses the axes. We will see some examples later.

problem.paragraph: ⓐ the zeros of the function, ⓑ any x-intercepts of the graph of the function, ⓒ any y-intercepts of the graph of the function

solution.paragraph: ⓐ To find the zeros of the function, we need to find when the function value is 0.

row.cell: Use the zero product property. Solve.

solution.paragraph: ⓑ An x-intercept occurs when $$y = 0.$$ Since $$f(-4) = 0$$ and $$f\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) = 0,$$ the points $$\left( {-4,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {\frac{2}{3},0} \right)$$ lie on the graph. These points are x-intercepts of the function. ⓒ A y-intercept occurs when $$x = 0.$$ To find the y-intercepts we need to find $$f(0).$$
Since $$f(0) = -8,$$ the point $$\left( {0,-8} \right)$$ lies on the graph. This point is the y-intercept of the function.

section.heading: Solve Applications Modeled by Polynomial Equations
section.paragraph: The problem-solving strategy we used earlier for applications that translate to linear equations will work just as well for applications that translate to polynomial equations. We will copy the problem-solving strategy here so we can use it for reference.

note.title: How To
note.heading: Use a problem solving strategy to solve word problems.

list.item: Step 1. Read the problem. Make sure all the words and ideas are understood.
Step 2. Identify what we are looking for.
Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose a variable to represent that quantity.
Step 4. Translate into an equation. It may be helpful to restate the problem in one sentence with all the important information. Then, translate the English sentence into an algebraic equation.
Step 5. Solve the equation using appropriate algebra techniques.
Step 6. Check the answer in the problem and make sure it makes sense.
Step 7. Answer the question with a complete sentence.

section.paragraph: The next example uses the function that gives the height of an object as a function of time when it is thrown from 80 feet above the ground.

problem.paragraph: Dennis is going to throw his rubber band ball upward from the top of a campus building. When he throws the rubber band ball from 80 feet above the ground, the function $$h(t) = -16t^{2} + 64t + 80$$ models the height, h, of the ball above the ground as a function of time, t. Find:
ⓐ the zeros of this function which tell us when the ball hits the ground, ⓑ when the ball will be 80 feet above the ground, ⓒ the height of the ball at $$t = 2$$ seconds.

solution.paragraph: ⓐ The zeros of this function are found by solving $$h(t) = 0.$$ This will tell us when the ball will hit the ground.

row.cell: Use the Zero Product Property. Solve.

solution.paragraph: The result $$t = 5$$ tells us the ball will hit the ground 5 seconds after it is thrown. Since time cannot be negative, the result $$t = -1$$ is discarded.
ⓑ The ball will be 80 feet above the ground when $$h(t) = 80.$$

row.cell: Use the Zero Product Property. Solve.
The ball will be at 80 feet the moment Dennis tosses the ball and then 4 seconds later, when the ball is falling.

solution.paragraph: ⓒ To find the height ball at $$t = 2$$ seconds we find $$h(2).$$

row.cell: After 2 seconds, the ball will be at 144 feet.
